The heart stops on the table. It is the second time this heart has stopped, though only one of those times belongs to the man it lives in now. The other belongs to a man who was standing at a crossing with his daughters.

A mathematician lies in a hospital bed listening to a sound in his chest that did not come from his body. He cannot stop thinking about whose it was. He pays a man in a car park to find out, is told it is against every rule there is, and pays him anyway, and is handed a name and a street.

His wife sits across a kitchen table with a clinic form. What is in the freezer is all there will ever be. She wants the child more than she wants the marriage. He tells her he is not coming back and that he does not want the child, and she says the thing that is true: he is spending a life somebody else paid for.

A woman does the school run. She keeps the garden. She has not had anything in her system for years. Two girls and a husband who adores her, in a house with a fixed rate on it. She is taken into a side room off a corridor and told about her husband, and then, while she is still on the first thing, about both children. She starts again in the bathroom of a bar with the door locked, and then in the house, and then at the kitchen table with the girls' drawings still on the wall behind her.

An ex-convict with scripture inked up both forearms holds down a job, runs a boys' team on Saturdays, and testifies to anyone who will sit still. His wife watches the certainty in him the way you watch weather coming. The faith and the temper are the same thing wearing different clothes. His pickup comes through a crossing at the wrong moment and takes a man and two children off their feet. It goes on a hundred yards, stops, sits there with the engine running, backs up a little, and then goes. He walks up the steps of a police station on his own, waits at the counter, and tells the desk sergeant what he did. He is back inside. Released on somebody's recommendation, he gets as far as the gate, looks at the family waiting for him, and keeps walking. He takes a job cleaning rooms at a motel four hundred miles from any of it.

The mathematician follows the widow for a week, learns which pool she swims at, and arranges to be in the water at the same hour until it stops being a coincidence. Within a fortnight he is in her house. He says it in her kitchen, badly: what is beating in his chest came out of her husband. She puts him out that night with everything he brought. She asks him to come back, and he does.

She says she cannot go on breathing in the same country as the man who drove away from the crossing. She keeps saying it until it is the only thing in the house. He buys a pistol from a man in a lock-up and drives out to the motel with it under the seat. He gets the other man against a wall in the dark behind the building and cannot make his hand do it. The shot goes somewhere it will not kill. He stands over him telling him to get up and run.

The other man follows them back to their own room, bleeding through his shirt, and stands in the doorway asking to be finished. The mathematician turns the gun round and puts it into his own chest instead.

They get him into a car and drive with the horn down. The borrowed heart stops on the table anyway. The man who drove away from the crossing goes back to the family he walked out on. The woman goes home on her own carrying something.

A doctor shows a man the numbers and tells him the muscle is finished, that it will be weeks rather than months, and that the only thing that helps is somebody else dying at the right time. Somewhere in the same building a chest is opened and a heart that was beating an hour ago in somebody else is put into it. He wakes in the night able to breathe, and lies there listening to it.

Inside his own head, Tobias stood in the worst of it—the shouting, the silences, the door—and watched each room lose its walls while he was still in it. The ugly part was going first.

Two technicians had let themselves into his flat at night, put the cap on him while he slept, and worked through the map room by room. One of them, a young man named Peck, quietly slipped the bagged keepsakes into his own coat.

When the machine reached the memories he wanted to keep, Tobias started to run. He carried her out of her own memories and into places she was never in—a childhood kitchen, under a table, somewhere the map did not go.

He had filled two carrier bags with everything that had her in it—a hairslide, a mug, a page torn out of something—so the machine could find the memories they were pinned to. He had handed them over willingly.

The two on the outside were drinking his beer and dancing on his bed in their underwear when the map on the screen stopped corresponding to anything. Neither noticed for a long time.

He had walked into the director's office that afternoon and asked for the same thing. That afternoon if possible. He had the form letter the clinic sent to everyone she knew.

The director arrived at three in the morning to put the thing back on the rails. The receptionist kissed him in the hallway, and his wife, coming in behind him, told her exactly why she had always felt that way about him and could not remember why.

He had gone to the bookshop to make it up with her. She looked at him the way you look at a customer. There was a young man behind the counter, and she was laughing at everything he said.

The last thing left was the shore house on the night they met. In the doorway of a room that was already going,

Ash drove the way a man drives when the back seat is screaming. He took the corner into the yard on two wheels, hauled the door open, and pulled Elm out of the car by the jacket. The man's shirt was black and wet and his legs folded the moment they touched concrete. Ash carried him the way you carry someone who is already half gone, laid him on the loading ramp, and put a hand behind his head.

You're not dying, he said. Nobody dies here today.

Elm's mouth opened and nothing came out but a sound like tearing paper.

What happened to you, Ash said. What did you do.

It had gone wrong inside a minute. The alarm was already running when they came through the door, and Ash had fired through the windscreen and out of both side windows while the car went the wrong way down a one-way street. Elm had gotten clear on foot, run two blocks, and dragged a woman out of her car at a junction. She had a pistol in the door pocket. She put one round into his stomach before he could close the door. He shot her. He drove three streets bleeding from the wound and the guilt both, and then Ash found him.

Now Ash held him on the ramp and said it again. Nobody dies.

The door opened and Birch came in clean and furious. He walked the room, counted heads, and said what they were all thinking. The police were on the pavement before the first alarm. Timings don't lie. One of us called it in. Then he went back outside with the stones and came back empty-handed, and nobody asked where he'd put them because nobody wanted to know.

Ash barely heard him. He was pressing his jacket into Elm's wound and the jacket was drinking it.

The door opened again and Cedar strolled in unhurried, complained about the noise, and then went back to his car and opened the boot. He dragged out a young patrolman in uniform with his hands cable-tied behind him. The officer's name was Doyle and he was perhaps twenty-three years old and he was about to have the worst afternoon of his short life.

Cedar had walked out of prison that morning into an envelope and a place on the crew, because Bram owed him for years of keeping his mouth shut. That was the kind of man he was. The kind who takes the debt and then takes a prisoner for the pleasure of it, because the debt was never the point.

He left Doyle on a chair and turned the radio up. Something from twenty years ago. He danced a few steps to it, took a razor out, and cut the officer's ear off. He talked into the ear like it was a telephone. Then he poured petrol over the man from a can he'd brought in his boot, and Doyle's screaming became something else entirely.

From the floor, Elm raised his gun and emptied it into Cedar's chest.

The radio kept playing. Elm dropped the gun and looked at Doyle and said: I'm a police officer. There are cars outside waiting for Bram. You hold on. You hold on.

He had rehearsed for this. In a safe room with his handler Pruitt, he had told a story about a drug bust in a public toilet so many times that it stopped being a story and became a memory. Four dogs, a bag of pills, a wet floor. He told it until Pruitt said stop, you're remembering it now, not reciting it. Then he walked into a bar and told it to Bram and Cal and Ash, got the laugh in the right place, and walked out with a job and a name he hadn't picked. That was how long he had been lying to every person in the building.

Eight men in black suits had eaten breakfast together in a diner, arguing about a pop song and whether a waitress deserved a tip, and none of them had used a real name. Bram had dealt out tree names from a list so no man could give up another. Birch had argued about being Birch. Nobody had argued about being Elm, because Elm hadn't known he was Elm yet.

Cal came back to a body on the floor and a story about Cedar. He listened. He looked at the officer on the chair. He put three rounds into Doyle's chest and closed the matter.

Then Bram walked in.

He looked at Elm on the ramp for a long moment. Then he said: This is the one.

Ash put his gun on Bram. He would not be told otherwise. Three guns came up in a room the size of a garage and all three went off. When it stopped, Bram and Cal were dead and Ash and Elm were still breathing, barely, on the wet floor beside each other.

Elm turned his head. He said it plainly because the man had earned it. I'm a police officer. My name is Danny Roarke.

Ash dragged himself up, put the gun to Danny's head, and the doors came in as he fired.

The gun dealer did an impression of the accent for the benefit of nobody. Nadir stood at the counter with his daughter Sahar translating, and he paid and left armed and humiliated. He could not have known that months from now he would stand outside a locksmith's house in the dark with that same pistol raised, shouting, and that a small girl would come off the porch at a run and be in her father's arms just as it went off. He could not have known that nothing would happen—that the child would not be marked, and neither would her father, because Sahar, asked to buy a box of ammunition, had quietly bought the box that does nothing. He would call the child an angel. But that was later.

Trey and Kwame walked up a restaurant pavement talking about who was watching them, then produced pistols and took a prosecutor's car off Halstead and his wife Paula on the kerb. What neither of them could see was a detective standing over a body face down in the mud by a roadside, walking over with his hands in his pockets and then stopping, because he knew the shoes. The man in the first car would be somebody's brother. But that was later.

Officer Boyle pulled the Hobarts over for nothing, had them out on the bonnet, and searched Renee with his hand where it did not need to go while her husband Clay stood three feet away and said nothing. What Renee could not know was that one night she would be hanging upside down in a car on its roof with petrol running toward a fire, and the man who crawled in through the gap and got her belt off would be the one who put his hand up her skirt. Her life would be owed to the man who assaulted her. But that was later.

The next morning Boyle's partner Voss went to their commander and said he could not ride with the man anymore. He was told he could have a new car if he said the problem was flatulence, and he took the deal. He thought that settled it.

Mateo changed the Halsteads' locks while Paula stood at the top of the stairs telling her husband, at volume, that the tattooed one would be selling their keys to his friends by morning. The fear of the carjacking discharged onto the nearest brown man. Later Mateo fitted a new lock on Nadir's shop and told him the lock was never the problem—the door itself needed replacing. Nadir heard a man inventing a second job and ordered him out.

Boyle sat across a desk pleading with a health insurance clerk named Delia Frank for a referral for his old man who could not pass water without weeping. He got a flat no and lost it entirely at the name on her badge. The cruelty had a shape and an origin, and neither excused it.

The door came off its hinges exactly as predicted. The stock was destroyed, the walls were written on, and the insurer declined on the grounds that Nadir had been warned about the door.

The stolen car caught a small man crossing between parked vans and folded him over the bonnet. Trey and Kwame argued about it for two streets and left him breathing outside a hospital entrance.

Clay was dragged out of his own car at gunpoint by four officers who had been told it was stolen. Voss walked into the middle of it and got him home. Clay drove away from the roadblock at a speed neither of them enjoyed with Trey crouched in the passenger seat, then pulled over three miles later and put him out on the verge without a word.

Voss picked up a young man walking in the rain. They got on. A hand went into a pocket for something, and the officer who asked for a different partner put two rounds into Kwame and drove the body out to a ditch and burned the car.

Reece was called out to the body. He knew the shoes. His mother was on the kitchen floor when he told her, and what came back was that she had asked him a hundred times to go and look for his brother and he never once went.

Paula went over on the top step with nobody in the house and lay there until her housekeeper Alba found her. In the ambulance she told the only person who came that she was the best friend she had.

Trey bought the wrecked van cheap, opened the back expecting stock, and found two dozen people sitting in the dark who had been paid for. He drove them to the docks, gave them what was in his pocket, and told them to go.

Snow started over the city for the first time that winter. Two cars touched at a junction, both drivers got out, and the shouting started before either of them had looked at the damage.

On the morning he turned twenty-five, Emmett Rusk took control of the fortune and told the banker Barrow that of all his holdings he wanted only the failing city newspaper, the Clarion. He said it might be fun.

Barrow had come west twenty years earlier to collect the boy. A lodger who could not pay his board had left a mine deed behind, and the seam under it had turned out enormous. At the kitchen table in the boarding house, Emmett's mother signed her son and the money over to the banker while the boy's father objected from the doorway and was ignored. Out in the snow, the boy drove his sled into Barrow's stomach hard enough to sit the man down, and was taken east that evening regardless. The sled was painted with a name: Bluebell.

Emmett moved into the Clarion offices, installed his manager Marsh and his friend Devlin beside him, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page over his own name. He hired away the entire staff of the rival paper by paying them more and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line, dancing in the middle of it himself.

He returned from a buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. The wedding was on every front page but his own. Then the breakfasts began to lengthen—the talk shortening, the table growing, until the two of them sat at either end reading rival newspapers, one of which he owned.

He met Nora Kell on a street corner, mud on his coat, both of them laughing. He started visiting her rooms in secret and told nobody. Ten days before the ballot, the party boss Halloran brought Adele up the stairs to those rooms and offered a straight trade: withdraw on grounds of health, or be on every front page by Monday. Emmett told him to get out of the building. He lost the election. The Clarion printed FRAUD AT THE POLLS across six columns. Devlin asked to be transferred to another city. Adele went without either of them raising a voice.

He married Nora and bought her a teacher, a house to sing in, a career for which she had no voice. The debut was a humiliation. Devlin, brought back to cover it, got drunk and fell asleep over half a savage paragraph. Emmett finished the sentence in the same direction, set it, printed it, and fired him. Nora swallowed poison rather than sing again. When she could speak she said she would rather have died. He told her she may stop.

He shut her away in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, where the ceilings were too high to heat and the crates were never unpacked. She worked jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall the size of a station. After a joyless picnic on a black beach and a quarrel that carried through the canvas, she packed in the morning. He told her she could not go. She went.

He wrecked her bedroom with his hands and stopped at a glass snow globe. He murmured one word to nobody—Bluebell—and carried it past facing mirrors that gave back an old man repeated until he was too small to see. Alone at Silvermount, he died with the word on his lips and let the globe go. It rolled off the boards and broke on the step.

A newsreel obituary recapped his public life and closed without explaining his last word. The reporter Nash was sent to find out what it meant. He started with Nora, drunk at a seaside nightclub at four in the afternoon, who told him to get out before he finished the sentence. He read Barrow's memoir in a marble library. He interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora again, and the butler Colm. He put his notebook away and said no single word explains a life. Below him, workmen cleared the hall of crates and shoveled a small sled marked Bluebell into the furnace.

For six months he had not slept. Then he found that an hour in a church hall listening to people describe what was killing them, and being held afterward by one of them, bought him a full night's unconsciousness. He went four evenings a week. He wept at diseases he did not have and it was the only honest thing left in him, and he slept.

A woman started turning up in the same folding chairs. She smoked through the meditation. She was faking, and the moment he could see the lie in her he could see it in himself, and the sleep stopped. Her name was Ada Vey.

On a night flight for work he sat next to a soap salesman named Rex Marrow who talked for forty minutes about how everything either of them owned had been chosen for them by someone else. He pocketed the card. Later, standing at a phone box with his flat's windows on the pavement and every piece of catalogue furniture gone with them, he did not ring the woman. He rang the salesman. Rex took him to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district, a place with no working plumbing and a kitchen that smelled of tallow.

In the car park outside a bar Rex handed him a beer and asked, quite seriously, to be hit as hard as he could. They went at each other on the tarmac until neither could stand and both were laughing. He had never felt anything so clearly.

Later — much later, in a service stairwell of a tower he would not know the purpose of for months — he would be beaten down those same concrete steps a flight at a time by a man who was not there, and at the bottom he would put a gun in his own mouth and angle it and fire through his cheek to kill someone who had never been separate from him. But that was later. In the car park it was still just two men, and the feeling was clean.

The brawling hardened into a weekly thing in a cellar. Rules were read aloud at the start. The cellar filled. There was a waiting list.

Ada overdosed. Rex brought her back to the derelict house, and for weeks the two of them were audible through every floor while he lay rigid downstairs. At the same time Rex was boiling down fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic's bins, cutting it into bars, selling it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. The operation had an income.

One night Rex held his hand flat on the kitchen table, tipped lye onto the back of it, and would not let him retreat into counting breaths or going to the cave in his mind. The scar would still be there at the end — at a high window, his face wrapped in gauze, holding Ada's hand while the buildings came down one after another in order. But that was later. In the kitchen he learned only that he was not allowed to leave his own body any more.

He walked into his employer's office and said what he wanted. When he was refused he beat his own face into the carpet and let security find them. He was paid to stay away. The operation had a salary.

The cellar became a name — Havoc — and a shaved head and a doctrine. The house filled with young men who slept on the floor and went out at night to break things belonging to companies. It was no longer his, and he could not say when it had stopped being.

Rex took both hands off the wheel on a wet road, asked the men in the back what they wished they had done, and let the car go into the oncoming lane. When the narrator came round in the ditch, Rex was not there and was not anywhere.

A member named Ogden was shot dead coming out of a job with a drill in his hand. The house recited his name all night. The narrator started trying to shut the thing down.

He flew city to city. The same cellar under every bar. The same rules on the same wall. Barmen and desk clerks who looked up and called him Rex Marrow.

In a motel room with the flight records and the receipts spread over the bed, it went together. One body. One bank account. Every conversation between the two of them held in an empty room.

He got Ada on the telephone and asked whose bed she had been in. She said his, obviously. The last thing he was holding on to went.

He found the vans in the car parks beneath the towers that held every record of who owed what, wired and timed. He tried to defuse them. Rex beat him down the stairwell. He put the gun in his mouth and fired.

Ada was delivered by the shaven men, who apologised and left. The two of them stood at the window holding hands, and outside the buildings went down.

Above the noise, at an open window, an old man is telling a younger one that nothing anybody does survives. He says it is not a complaint but a fact. Below them, the street is full of blue light.

Two men are being carried out of a basement club with their hands behind them. One is shouting, the other is silent. Police shoulder them through the crowd and into the waiting car. The shouting one has an arm that bends where arms are not meant to bend.

Inside the club, a fire extinguisher lies on the floor beside a man who has stopped moving. The man with the extinguisher had gone on swinging long after there was any need to. A few feet away, watching with everyone else, stood the man they had actually come for. He watched the wrong man die and he did nothing, because there was nothing for him to do. The night had solved his problem for him.

The wrong man had been chosen because the one with the broken arm had gone through the club pulling faces out of the dark until he picked one. He had seized the man's collar and shouted a name at him. The man he had seized took his arm at the elbow and turned it until something came apart. That was when the other one took the extinguisher off the wall.

They had known to come to this club because of two men in a doorway on the side street. The two men had detached themselves from the wall and offered, for money, to say who had done it and where he drank. They pointed down the street towards the basement club and took the money and were gone.

Before that, the two of them had come out of a party still half-laughing, and stopped. There was a trolley on the pavement, and a blanket, and a face on it that they both knew. The laughing stopped. One of them said her name. Neither of them had known what had happened while they were inside.

What had happened was this. She had left the party on her own because the road was four lanes of headlights and she could not cross, so she took the stairs down into a pedestrian underpass instead. Halfway along the tiled tunnel a man had a woman by the hair and was explaining something to her with his fist. The man turned and saw Lise standing there. He did not hurry. He turned the violence onto her without changing his expression, and when it was over he went on hitting her head against the concrete floor. At the far end of the tunnel a man looked, hesitated, and left. Nobody came down the stairs.

She had been walking alone because she had collected her coat and gone out. Inside, the one she lived with had drunk past the point of being any fun and started working the room, pursuing women he did not know. She had watched him for a while, said nothing, and left. The man she used to live with was still inside and had not noticed.

The three of them had arrived together, standing swaying in the underground carriage, arguing cheerfully about sex and about how much he had already had to drink. It was the argument of people who expected to be arguing again tomorrow. They had been in good humour then.

Earlier that same afternoon she had been lying on her side in a park with a book she was not really reading. Sprinklers turned over cut grass and children ran through the spray. She had one hand resting flat on her stomach. The day had begun in complete safety.

That morning she had sat on the edge of the bath with the stick held in both hands, alone in the flat. She had let herself smile at it before she had told anyone at all. Positive. She had told nobody.

And before that, in the first light through thin curtains, she had lain in bed with Cort describing a recurring dream. A red tunnel she kept walking into. The two of them had teased each other about her ex-boyfriend Jonah, who was now only a friend. They had been easy with one another. The tunnel in the dream was red, and it frightened her, and she had laughed when she said so.

All night the helicopters came low over the roofs, spraying for crop pests, putting poison on the fruit fly and on everybody's washing, and every household in the city heard the same noise at the same hour.

Doctor Neil Hartigan changed his shirt twice. His wife Bess painted until the last minute in a studio full of unfinished bodies. Neither was enthusiastic about the guest list for the dinner party they were preparing, but they went on preparing it.

Across town the baker Otto Kemp took an order from a woman called Elaine for a birthday cake. She chose a design from a book and wrote a name on a card: Charlie Rill, age eight. Kemp said it would be ready Monday, and to collect it promptly.

On Monday, Charlie stepped off the kerb on his way to school. A waitress called Rhona, in a hurry, caught him with the wing of her car. He got up, said he was fine, refused a lift and walked home. He went to sleep on the sofa and did not wake up properly. After that there was a room with a machine in it and two parents taking shifts in a chair. Grant and Elaine kept vigil. In the corridor, Grant's estranged father Duff turned up with a coffee and, because he could not think of anything else to say into the silence, confessed an affair from decades ago.

Nobody collected the cake. Nobody paid for it. A man who was bad at being ignored began ringing the Rill house at two in the morning to say the boy's name into the dark.

In another living room Cheryl folded nappies with the receiver under her chin, describing things she was not doing to men she would never meet. Her husband Stu sat three feet away, getting quietly furious. On a Friday he and three friends drove two hours into the mountains to fish. They found a young woman face down in the shallows, pale and unhurried, exactly where they were going to stand. Somebody suggested she was not going anywhere and neither was the weekend. They put a line round her ankle to stop her drifting and carried on fishing for two more days before telling anyone. When Vern's wife Iris heard the story the way it was told at the pub, she stopped halfway through taking off her clown makeup, sponge still in her hand, and said nothing more that evening.

The singer Vida performed six nights a week under a low light, doing standards beautifully to people who were mostly talking. At home her cellist daughter Bee practised into an empty room.

Officer Rowe, cheating on his wife Peg with a woman called Nan, needed a reason to have been out. He drove the family dog to the far side of the valley and put it out of the car, and told Peg it must have got over the fence. Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned she had a new man and went to her house and sawed every chair, table and bedframe into pieces in an afternoon.

Ike and Dot house-sat for the Hartigans and photographed Dot made up as a beaten corpse, lying in the hall with pale foundation and bruises drawn on.

At the dinner party, over the fish, Bess admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and then the affair that came after it. Neil put his glass down very carefully and made a scene.

In the morning they switched off the machine. Charlie died. That afternoon Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery to confront Otto about the telephone calls. He sat them down, put warm bread in front of them, and grieved with them.

Bee came home from a rehearsal, found her mother asleep in the chair as usual, walked out to the garage, pulled the door down and started the car engine.

On a picnic in the hills, Stu smashed a young woman's head with a rock.

A tremor shook the entire city for about eleven seconds. By the evening bulletin every death and every wreck had been folded into the same three minutes of news.

Ruben shares the house with his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor's wife Alma and their baby. Four adults, a child and a rottweiler in a place built for two. He sleeps on the couch and watches Alma move through the kitchen.

Nestor robs a chemist's by night and comes home to knock her across the kitchen for asking where the money went. Ruben begins pressing her to leave with him, quietly at first and then not quietly.

The dog, Tigre, comes back off the street having killed something bigger than itself. A neighbour explains what that is worth. Within a month Tigre is going into a ring twice a week and coming out every time, and Ruben is saving.

He gives two men in a bar the address of his own brother. Nestor comes out of hospital, works out who arranged it in about a day, and leaves with Alma, the baby and every note hidden in the wardrobe.

The promoter Chaco loses too much on one fight and puts a pistol into Tigre's side in the middle of the ring. Ruben goes over the rope with a knife into him and is out the door and into the truck with Pipo before anyone moves. The truck comes through a red light at sixty with the dog bleeding across the back seat and takes the side out of a small car turning across the junction.

Nestor is shot dead robbing a bank with the same scarf. At the funeral Ruben makes the offer one last time, and Alma looks at him and says no and means it. Everything he did it for refuses him at the graveside.

A married man walks out on a wife and two daughters at a birthday party and moves the model Celine Vaz into a new flat with a floor-to-ceiling window, directly opposite the hoarding carrying her own face.

She wakes in hospital with a cage of steel pins holding her leg together and asks first about Chispa, her lapdog, which was alone in the new flat and has not been seen since.

Chispa falls through a hole in the floorboards. Her whining comes up through every room. Hector tears up the boards one by one with a crowbar while Celine's leg turns gangrenous above him.

The leg goes above the knee. In the same week the hoarding is stripped and pasted over with something else, and the two of them sit in the wrecked flat looking at a blank frame.

A vagrant pushing a cart of scrap through that same junction stands in the smoke, looks at the two wrecks and the people running towards them, and drags the bleeding dog out of the back seat and walks away with it.

Cardo gets Tigre back on its feet over weeks in a yard full of strays, feeding it by hand. It sleeps against him and follows him out into the street in the morning.

The businessman Elian meets him behind a church, hands him a photograph of his half-brother and business partner Sergio, and names a figure. Cardo takes half in advance and asks no questions.

He stands a long way back at his own wife's burial among people who think he died twenty years ago, then follows his grown daughter Perla through three streets and stops outside her building.

He comes home to a yard of dead dogs and Tigre standing in the middle of them with its muzzle wet. He puts the gun against its head, holds it there, and sits down on the ground.

He abducts Sergio off a pavement and chains him to a bed frame among the empty kennels instead of killing him. Then he brings Elian in, sits him opposite his brother, puts a loaded pistol on the floor between them, and walks out having taken money from both.

He breaks into Perla's flat, sits on her bed for an hour, and leaves a long confession on the answering machine saying who he is, where he went and why. He takes one photograph off the shelf.

Shaved, in clean clothes that do not fit him, he leaves the money on her table, takes the dog, and walks out across the flat grey ground at the edge of the city with nowhere in particular to be.

Solly Two Coats and his crew walked into the diamond house in the northern port dressed as devout pilgrims, heads bowed, prayer beads clicking between their fingers. The guards barely glanced at them. By the time the disguises hit the floor and the alarm shattered the afternoon, Solly was already outside with a stone the size of a pigeon's egg tucked against his palm. His telephone rang that evening. Marv, overseas, his cousin's voice flat and unsurprised, told him to bring it straight over. No delays, no stops, no cleverness. Solly agreed.

But cleverness was already in motion. Grigor the Nail, who worked every angle in the city's underworld, told Solly about a bookmaker's shop that would take a large wager no questions asked. Simultaneously, in a separate room, he tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno about the same bookmaker's—a fat target with a careless back door. Neither Solly nor the pawnbrokers knew the other was coming.

Across town, the boxing promoters Halloway and Digby had their own problems. They sent their fighter Pretty Sam to a travellers' camp to buy a caravan for transport to an upcoming bout. Sam treated the residents with open contempt, and a bare-knuckle fighter named Finn knocked him cold in the dirt. Halloway stared at his unconscious man and understood: he had no fighter for the gang boss Coldstone's fixed bout. He went to Coldstone's office and promised that Finn would go down in the fourth round. Coldstone nodded once.

Solly landed in the city and went first to the fence Hersch, handing over the stone for safekeeping. Then he carried his locked case to the bookmaker's, making himself visible, making himself a target. Ike, Benno, and a third man named Tulley burst in wearing masks. They seized Solly's arm and the case, fumbled through the alarms, and ran straight into Grigor, who chased them off with a drawn pistol. They escaped with the case and the man.

Finn knocked his opponent out in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune and took it out on Halloway with his fists.

Marv flew in, found no Solly and no stone, and hired a bounty hunter named Ledge to find them both. Ledge's method was simple: follow the least competent people in the chain.

Grigor took Solly to a workshop and cut off his arm to open the case. It was empty. The stone had never been inside it. Ledge traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces on a city street, and took both men and the diamond they had retrieved from Hersch. Coldstone fed what remained of Solly to his pigs. He showed Halloway and Digby the pens and told them what would happen if the second fight went wrong.

Halloway and Digby told Finn to go down in the fourth. That night, Coldstone's men went to the travellers' camp and burned Finn's mother to death in her caravan.

Grigor ambushed Ledge's car on a city road. In the shootout, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. Tulley, who had been following at a distance, got away with a dog that had swallowed the diamond days earlier without anyone noticing.

Finn waited until the fourth round, just as instructed, and knocked his opponent out cold. The travellers rose from their seats throughout the crowd and massacred Coldstone's men. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone alone in the chaos and shot him. By morning the travellers had vanished.

The dog was handed in at a pet shop a week later. It coughed up the diamond on the examination table. Halloway and Digby, who had come to collect it through a quiet arrangement with the shop's owner, stood holding the stone that had traveled through so many hands and never once belonged to them. They looked at each other. Then they locked the door.

Emlyn sat in Wilder's front room and said it as though he were correcting a minor point of fact. He had known for four years. Odile had told him on the trip abroad, the one Wilder remembered only as a fortnight when her letters had stopped. And the letters themselves—Emlyn had read those too, the ones Wilder had sent to the hotel, held at the desk in her name. He had never thought much of them, he added, in the same level tone. Wilder stood by the cold fireplace and felt the floor give way beneath a structure he had believed solid for years.

He had telephoned Emlyn that same evening, still in a state, still turning over what Odile had told him the night before in a bar. She had said her marriage was over. She had said she had finally confessed everything to Emlyn—the affair, the rooms, all of it—and that the confession had ended things between them. Wilder had listened with the careful attention of a man hearing a story whose first chapter he could not quite recall. Then she had let slip, almost as an afterthought, that Emlyn had been publishing a novelist Wilder represented, a man they had once agreed over dinner was a fraud. The two men had carried on a professional relationship neither had mentioned. What else had been concealed? Wilder had gone home and dialled the number he knew by heart.

Two years before that telephone call, Wilder and Odile had sat in a bar and she had spoken as though the ground were only now breaking. The marriage was ending. She had told Emlyn everything the previous night. Wilder nodded, but the word *everything* unsettled him, because it implied a before and after he could not locate. She made it sound as though Emlyn had learned only then, as though the years of lunches and dinners and racquet-game conversations had been conducted in genuine ignorance.

Before the bar, before the confession she believed was the first, there had been the closing of the rooms. They had split the crockery and surrendered the lease not because anyone had found them out but because the afternoons had become a chore. The linen had lost its charge.
